## Plugin reference

- Description: Global toast notifications: a plain showToast() (text toasts: data only) backed by sonner's global API, and useShowCustomToast() — a toast whose content the caller draws, rendered in the caller's render origin (its transport, registry and navigator) while the stack only places it, plus the Core.Root-mounted sonner Toaster host. Degrades to a silent no-op when no host is mounted. A toast declaring audience developer is shown only in Developer mode. isPageOnScreen() gates a toast nobody asked for (an announcement: a notification arriving, a reconnect) — sonner keeps a hidden page's toasts mounted until it is shown. useSuppressToasts() lets a surface that is its whole document (the menu-bar panel) turn the host off while mounted.

## Announcements: only on a page on screen

A toast is either an answer to something the user did (Copied, a failed
save: raised whatever the page's state, the user is waiting for it) or an
announcement of something that happened on its own (a notification arriving,
the server reconnecting). An announcement is raised only while
`isPageOnScreen()` is true; its record lives on its persistent surface (the
bell's row and unread badge).

Why: sonner pauses every toast's dismiss timer while the document is hidden
and keeps every toast in its list mounted (only the front three are drawn),
so a toast raised in a hidden tab stays until the tab is shown. Before this
rule a background tab kept one toast per notification. Measured per arrival on
a hidden page: +35 DOM nodes, +28 layout objects, +146 event listeners (each
custom toast is its own React root). On 2026-11-14 that added ~12k nodes per
tab in 2 h and took one Chrome renderer with 6 equin tabs from 3.3 GB to
10.4 GB (report-1794679800-lyevgy).

## Click-to-dismiss

Clicking a toast anywhere dismisses it — except a click that ends a text
selection (so its words can be copied), and a click on a control inside it (a
button, link or input: its action, a custom toast's ×, a popover trigger),
which is the control's own: it acts, and dismisses itself if it means to. The
check runs in the body's native `<li>` listener (`isControlClick`), not by the
control stopping propagation, which from React would come too late.
